item: Know who is at risk, ward by ward
eg: Thane, India, built a ward-level risk index that combines felt heat, warm nights and social vulnerability.

Singapore’s national heat stress advisory uses wet-bulb globe temperature, which counts humidity, sun and wind, with three risk levels. In a 2023 review, only about 10 of 37 Indian heat plans appeared to set local thresholds.
Dhaka North found hotspots more than 10 °C hotter than the surrounding countryside; Cooling Singapore models where heat builds up, street by street.

item: Count lost work and wages, not only illness
eg: The World Bank estimates heat cost Bangladesh 250 million workdays in 2024, worth up to US$1.78 billion.
Singapore requires hourly heat checks on outdoor worksites and at least 10 minutes’ shaded rest each hour for heavy work when wet-bulb globe temperature reaches 32 °C, and inspects for it.

item: Give every department a role for each season
eg: Thane’s heatwave task force is chaired by an Additional Municipal Commissioner; Tamil Nadu convened a Heat Action Network of state departments.
Nepal’s Madhesh Province and five of its municipalities committed 5% of sectoral budgets to adaptation and disaster risk reduction, with support from Practical Action and Mercy Corps.
In April 2024 the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society activated its heatwave early action protocol for Dhaka before the peak: warnings, drinking water, cooling stations and cash.

item: Tie work rules to heat alerts
eg: Since 2023, Spain has required employers to cut or move working hours when the weather agency issues an orange or red heat alert and other measures can’t keep workers safe.
